tasks.prompt: Ultrafiltration Train 2 transmembrane pressure rose 38 percent in 10 days at constant flux while Train 1 stayed stable.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 3 water treatment plant log. Steady flow unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and maintenance records are available for review.

Chemically enhanced backwash recovery on Train 2 fell from 92 percent to 61 percent, while Train 1 stayed at 91 percent.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Biofouling on Train 2 is driving the TMP rise
Irreversible mineral scaling is driving the TMP rise on both trains
Feed pump wear is reducing flux on Train 2
The TMP transmitter on Train 2 has drifted high

inference.explanation: The rise is train specific at constant flux and temperature, which rules out a plant wide scaling or pump cause. High plate counts plus strong recovery from a chlorine soak and poor recovery from acid fit biofouling, not mineral scale. A drifted transmitter would not change backwash recovery or bench soak results.

options.label: Archived ATP and plate count trend paired with TMP trend for each train
Archived feed pump amperage log
Archived raw water hardness log

nextClue.explanation: Comparing biological counts with TMP by train tests whether biological growth tracks the pressure rise.

clueText.nc-b: Pump amperage was steady on both trains and does not separate the trains.
clueText.nc-c: Hardness was steady and does not explain a train specific biological signal.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The plant can support 3 log credit, but records do not support the claimed 4 log credit
A membrane breach occurred and was hidden
The turbidimeter limit means no removal occurred
Missing records prove the plant was shut down

inference.explanation: Passing tests support removal only to the sensitivity actually demonstrated, which is 3 log. Missing records and coarse turbidity resolution mean 4 log is unsupported, but passing particle counts argue against claiming a breach or zero removal occurred.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best resolves the credit question?

options.label: Archived integrity test sensitivity calculation paired with the daily test log
Archived permeate storage volume log
Archived operator shift roster

nextClue.explanation: Sensitivity calculations plus the test log show what removal the testing can actually verify.

clueText.nc-a: Sensitivity math caps verifiable removal at 3 log and two days lack tests, so 4 log cannot be credited.
clueText.nc-b: Storage volume does not set integrity credit.
clueText.nc-c: The roster does not change test sensitivity.

tasks.prompt: A trial raised ultrafiltration backwash frequency from every 30 minutes to every 20 minutes and net plant output fell, prompting a review.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 3 water treatment plant log. Steady flow unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and maintenance records are available for review.

evidence.label: Gross permeate production rose 1 percent with the more frequent backwash.
Backwash waste volume rose from 3 percent to 6.5 percent of gross production.
TMP rise per day was unchanged between the two settings in a paired 2 week trial.
Chemical use and energy per net cubic metre both rose in the trial period.
Feed turbidity was matched between the trial and baseline periods.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The extra backwashing wastes more water than it recovers, with no fouling benefit at this feed quality
More frequent backwash always improves net output
The trial feed water was dirtier, hiding a real benefit
Backwash waste is not counted in net output

inference.explanation: With matched feed quality, TMP behaviour was unchanged while waste volume more than doubled, so net output fell. The small gross gain cannot offset the waste increase, which the per net volume chemical and energy figures confirm.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best confirms the trial conclusion?

options.label: Archived net water recovery calculation for the paired trial periods
Archived backwash pump nameplate photo
Archived raw water colour log

nextClue.explanation: Net recovery math for matched periods is the direct measure of the change.

clueText.nc-a: Net recovery fell from 96.8 percent to 93.4 percent with no change in daily TMP rise.
clueText.nc-b: A nameplate photo does not measure trial performance.
clueText.nc-c: Colour was matched and does not change the recovery result.

tasks.prompt: Hollow fibre fouling accelerated after maintenance, with TMP rising twice as fast in the lower half of each module.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 3 water treatment plant log. Steady flow unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and maintenance records are available for review.

evidence.label: Air scour blower discharge pressure is normal at the header.
Individual module air flow checks show the bottom distribution laterals deliver 40 percent of design air.
A removed lateral shows biofilm and grit blocking most air holes.
Water only backwash recovery is unchanged from baseline.
Top half fibre permeability after cleaning is near baseline, while bottom half stays low.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Blocked air distribution laterals are starving the lower modules of scour air
The blower has lost capacity
The membranes have reached end of life
Feed turbidity doubled

inference.explanation: Header pressure is normal but module level air delivery is low, and the removed lateral is physically blocked, which localizes the fault to distribution, not the blower. Uneven top to bottom fouling matches uneven scour, not uniform end of life decline.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best confirms the air distribution fault?

options.label: Archived module by module air flow test results before and after lateral cleaning
Archived blower motor hour log
Archived permeate turbidity log

nextClue.explanation: Module level air flows before and after cleaning directly test the distribution fault.

clueText.nc-a: Bottom lateral flows rose to design after cleaning and TMP rise per day fell by half.
clueText.nc-b: Motor hours do not measure air delivery per module.
clueText.nc-c: Permeate turbidity does not locate an air fault.

tasks.prompt: Membrane fouling worsened after the upstream coagulant dose was raised to improve settled turbidity.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 3 water treatment plant log. Steady flow unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and maintenance records are available for review.

evidence.label: Settled turbidity improved from 2.0 NTU to 1.1 NTU after the dose increase.
Membrane feed residual aluminum rose from 0.05 mg/L to 0.31 mg/L.
Jar tests show the new dose is past the optimum and restabilizes fine particles at low temperature.
CIP waste from the membranes is high in aluminum hydroxide.
Returning the dose to the jar test optimum in a 1 week trial cut the TMP rise rate by 60 percent.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Excess coagulant carryover is fouling the membranes with aluminum hydroxide
The membranes are fouled by raw water algae
Higher coagulant dose always protects membranes
Settled turbidity improvement proves the dose is correct

inference.explanation: Residual aluminum in membrane feed and in CIP waste rose with the dose, and the dose reduction trial cut fouling sharply. Settled turbidity alone looks better, but jar tests show the dose is past optimum, so carryover, not algae, fits all records.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best confirms carryover fouling?

options.label: Archived membrane feed residual aluminum trend paired with the dose log
Archived raw water algae count log
Archived permeate flow totalizer log

nextClue.explanation: Residual aluminum tracking the dose log is the direct carryover test.

clueText.nc-a: Feed aluminum tracks dose changes within hours and falls when dose returns to optimum.
clueText.nc-b: Algae counts were low during the fouling period.
clueText.nc-c: Flow totals do not identify the foulant.

tasks.prompt: Permeate conductivity on one reverse osmosis vessel is three times the array average while its permeate flow is also high.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 3 water treatment plant log. Steady flow unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and maintenance records are available for review.

evidence.label: Probing shows conductivity peaks at one tube sheet position in the vessel.
Other vessels on the same feed show normal conductivity and flow.
Feed conductivity and recovery are steady for the whole array.
Replacing the interconnect O ring at the high conductivity position normalizes that vessel in a test run.
Salt passage calculated for all other vessels is within normal limits.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: A damaged O ring is bypassing feed water into that vessel permeate
The membrane in every vessel has oxidized
Feed salinity rose for one vessel only
The conductivity meter reads the whole array high

inference.explanation: The fault is confined to one vessel and one position, and an O ring replacement fixes it, which fits mechanical bypass. Plant wide oxidation or a meter fault would affect all vessels, and vessels share the same feed.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best confirms the bypass?

options.label: Archived vessel probing profile before and after the seal repair
Archived feed conductivity log
Archived array total permeate flow log

nextClue.explanation: Probing profiles locate the leak position and verify the repair.

clueText.nc-a: Probing isolates one position and the profile is flat and normal after the seal change.
clueText.nc-b: Feed conductivity was steady and normal.
clueText.nc-c: Total flow does not locate a single vessel leak.

tasks.prompt: A hazard review rates the coagulant feed as a critical control point, and monitoring adequacy is being assessed.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 3 water treatment plant log. Steady flow unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and maintenance records are available for review.

evidence.label: Coagulant feed has a low flow alarm, but it is checked only once per shift.
A feed interruption of 40 minutes in a past event raised settled turbidity above the filter design limit before the next shift check.
Continuous streaming current and settled turbidity monitoring exist but are not alarmed.
A trial with alarmed continuous monitoring detects a simulated feed loss in 3 minutes.
Chemical day tank sizing gives 18 hours of storage, so supply is not the weak point.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Detection delay, not storage or supply, is the control weakness at this critical control point
The coagulant feed is not a critical control point
Once per shift checks are adequate detection
Unalarmed trends provide the same protection as alarms

inference.explanation: A real 40 minute interruption already exceeded downstream limits before a shift check caught it, storage is ample, and alarmed monitoring detects a simulated loss in minutes. The weakness is how fast a loss is seen, which is what control at a critical point requires.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best confirms the detection gap?

options.label: Archived past interruption timeline paired with the alarmed monitoring trial
Archived day tank capacity calculation
Archived chemical delivery schedule

nextClue.explanation: The timeline shows harm occurring inside the current detection interval.

clueText.nc-a: Settled turbidity passed the filter limit 25 minutes into the past interruption, 5 hours before the next scheduled check.
clueText.nc-b: Capacity confirms supply is not the issue.
clueText.nc-c: Deliveries were never interrupted.

tasks.prompt: Cartridge filters ahead of reverse osmosis now last 5 days instead of 30, and SDI values rose from 2 to 6.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 3 water treatment plant log. Steady flow unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and maintenance records are available for review.

evidence.label: Multimedia prefilter effluent turbidity rose from 0.3 NTU to 1.4 NTU.
Prefilter backwash records show backwash flow was cut to 60 percent of design to save water.
A core sample of prefilter media shows mudballs and channel cracks.
Differential pressure across the prefilter falls during runs, suggesting bypass through channels.
Restoring design backwash flow in a trial returned effluent turbidity to 0.4 NTU within 3 runs.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Inadequate prefilter backwash caused channeling and solids breakthrough to the cartridges
Cartridge quality from the supplier suddenly fell
SDI test technique alone explains the change
Reverse osmosis membranes are shedding particles backward

inference.explanation: Rising prefilter effluent turbidity, falling differential pressure during runs, mudballs, and recovery after restoring backwash flow all point to channeling from weak backwash. A cartridge defect would not raise prefilter effluent turbidity or SDI upstream of the cartridges.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best confirms prefilter channeling?

options.label: Archived prefilter effluent turbidity trend paired with backwash flow records
Archived cartridge purchase invoices
Archived permeate conductivity log

nextClue.explanation: Effluent quality paired with backwash flow tests the backwash adequacy link.

clueText.nc-a: Effluent turbidity rose as backwash flow was cut and recovered when full flow was restored.
clueText.nc-b: Invoices do not measure filtration performance.
clueText.nc-c: Permeate conductivity is downstream and does not diagnose the prefilter.

tasks.prompt: Polyamide reverse osmosis salt rejection fell from 98.5 percent to 94 percent over 2 months and did not recover after cleaning.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 3 water treatment plant log. Steady flow unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and maintenance records are available for review.

evidence.label: Feed free chlorine averaged 0.4 mg/L during the period because the dechlorination carbon bed was exhausted.
Carbon bed effluent chlorine breakthrough was logged but the alarm was set at 1.0 mg/L.
Cleaning restored flow but not salt rejection.
A new membrane element tested on the same feed with fresh carbon gives 98.6 percent rejection.
Feed pressure and recovery are unchanged.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Chlorine oxidation permanently damaged the membrane polymer
Reversible organic fouling is reducing rejection
Feed temperature rise explains the rejection loss
Cleaning chemicals were too weak

inference.explanation: Documented chlorine exposure, flow recovery without rejection recovery after cleaning, and normal rejection from a new element on protected feed fit permanent oxidation. Reversible fouling would recover with cleaning, and operating conditions are unchanged.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best confirms oxidation damage?

options.label: Archived carbon bed effluent chlorine trend paired with rejection trend
Archived cleaning chemical volume log
Archived feed pressure log

nextClue.explanation: Chlorine exposure tracking rejection loss is the direct oxidation test.

clueText.nc-a: Rejection fell steadily while carbon effluent chlorine stayed near 0.4 mg/L and stabilized on protected elements after the carbon change.
clueText.nc-b: Cleaning volumes were standard and cleaning did restore flow.
clueText.nc-c: Feed pressure was steady throughout.

tasks.prompt: Raising reverse osmosis recovery from 75 percent to 82 percent caused rapid tail element fouling, and a concentrate valve was blamed.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 3 water treatment plant log. Steady flow unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and maintenance records are available for review.

evidence.label: Concentrate conductivity rose as expected with higher recovery and osmotic pressure rose 15 percent.
Lead element performance stayed normal while tail elements lost flow.
Calculated calcium carbonate and silica indices in the concentrate both exceed saturation at 82 percent but not at 75 percent.
Returning to 75 percent recovery in a trial stopped the flow loss without any valve work.
The concentrate valve position and flow readings match the set recovery.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The higher recovery pushed concentrate chemistry past saturation limits in the tail elements
The concentrate valve malfunction caused the fouling
Lead elements are fouled first and worst
Silica and calcium indices are unrelated to recovery

inference.explanation: Tail only loss, saturation indices crossing limits only at the higher recovery, and recovery in the trial without valve work all fit a chemistry limit. The valve readings match setpoint, ruling out the valve theory.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best confirms the recovery limit?

options.label: Archived concentrate saturation index calculations at both recovery settings
Archived valve maintenance roster
Archived feed tank level log

nextClue.explanation: Index calculations at both settings show whether chemistry crossed saturation.

clueText.nc-a: Indices exceed saturation at 82 percent and sit below it at 75 percent, matching where fouling occurred.
clueText.nc-b: The roster does not measure concentrate chemistry.
clueText.nc-c: Tank level does not set scaling limits.

tasks.prompt: An ultrafiltration train was taken out of service for a suspected breach, but permeate quality records conflict with the alarm.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 3 water treatment plant log. Steady flow unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and maintenance records are available for review.

evidence.label: The alarm came from a permeate turbidimeter reading 0.45 NTU.
A handheld turbidimeter on a permeate grab sample reads 0.05 NTU.
Pressure decay test passes at 3 kPa in 5 minutes.
Particle counts in permeate are at baseline for intact trains.
The online turbidimeter sample line is found full of air bubbles from a leaking fitting.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Air bubbles in the sample line caused a false high turbidity alarm on an intact train
A major fibre breach occurred
Pressure decay testing missed a large breach
Grab samples always read lower than online meters

inference.explanation: Passing integrity testing, baseline particle counts, and a normal grab result all say the train is intact, while bubbles in the sample line explain a false optical reading. A large breach would raise particle counts and fail pressure decay.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best confirms the false alarm?

options.label: Archived paired online and grab turbidity log after the fitting repair
Archived feed turbidity log
Archived backwash count log

nextClue.explanation: Paired readings after repair test whether the online meter agrees once air is removed.

clueText.nc-a: After the fitting repair the online meter reads 0.05 NTU and matches grabs for 7 days.
clueText.nc-b: Feed turbidity does not test the permeate sample line.
clueText.nc-c: Backwash counts do not explain an optical alarm.

tasks.prompt: Membrane TMP rises every spring for 3 weeks then recovers, and staff propose year round higher chemical cleaning frequency.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 3 water treatment plant log. Steady flow unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and maintenance records are available for review.

evidence.label: Spring raw water shows algae counts 30 times winter values and elevated algal organic matter.
Spring CIP waste is high in organic carbon and polysaccharide indicators.
Winter CIP waste is mostly inorganic with low organics.
A spring only pretreatment trial with powdered activated carbon cut the TMP rise rate by 55 percent.
Year round weekly cleans in one trial year gave no winter benefit over monthly cleans.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Seasonal algal organic fouling drives the spring TMP rise, so targeted spring pretreatment fits better than year round cleaning
The membranes degrade and heal seasonally
Winter inorganic fouling is the main spring problem
More cleaning always helps regardless of season

inference.explanation: Spring foulant chemistry is organic, algae and algal organics peak in spring, and a spring pretreatment trial worked, while extra winter cleaning gave no benefit. The pattern is a seasonal foulant, not membrane self repair or winter scale.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best confirms the seasonal foulant?

options.label: Archived seasonal CIP waste analysis paired with raw algae counts
Archived annual cleaning chemical invoices
Archived permeate tank level log

nextClue.explanation: Seasonal foulant chemistry paired with source counts identifies the driver.

clueText.nc-a: Spring waste organics peak with algae counts, while winter waste stays inorganic.
clueText.nc-b: Invoices show cost, not foulant type.
clueText.nc-c: Tank level does not identify foulants.

tasks.prompt: Four membrane trains share a header, but Train 3 fouls twice as fast as the others at the same reported flux.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 3 water treatment plant log. Steady flow unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and maintenance records are available for review.

evidence.label: Flow verification with a portable meter shows Train 3 actually carries 18 percent more flow than its panel meter reports.
Panel meters on Trains 1, 2, and 4 agree with the portable meter within 2 percent.
Train 3 panel meter was replaced last year with a different pipe size setting left in its configuration.
Correcting the meter factor in a trial equalizes reported flows and Train 3 fouling rate then matches the others at true equal flux.
Feed water is common to all trains.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: A meter configuration error overloaded Train 3 above its reported flux
Train 3 membranes are defective
Train 3 receives dirtier feed water
Train 3 cleaning is less effective than other trains

inference.explanation: Portable verification shows real overload on one train, the settings error explains it, and correcting the factor normalizes fouling. Shared feed rules out dirtier water for one train, and a membrane defect would not be fixed by a meter correction.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best confirms the overload?

options.label: Archived portable flow verification log paired with panel readings by train
Archived membrane purchase records
Archived feed turbidity log

nextClue.explanation: Independent flow checks by train directly test reported versus actual flux.

clueText.nc-a: Only Train 3 disagrees with the portable meter, by 18 percent, matching its extra fouling.
clueText.nc-b: Purchase records do not measure flow.
clueText.nc-c: Feed is common and turbidity does not split by train.

tasks.prompt: Ultrafiltration permeability declines within each filtration cycle but fully recovers after every backpulse.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 3 water treatment plant log. Steady flow unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and maintenance records are available for review.

evidence.label: TMP rises steadily during each 30 minute cycle and resets to baseline after backpulse.
Daily CIP is not needed to hold weekly average permeability, which is stable.
Permeate turbidity stays at 0.04 NTU through the cycles.
Feed turbidity is elevated at 3.5 NTU during a runoff week.
Extending the cycle to 60 minutes in a trial doubles end of cycle TMP but backpulse still fully recovers it.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Reversible surface cake from high feed solids is forming and clearing each cycle
Irreversible pore blocking is progressing
A breach opens during filtration and seals at backpulse
Chemical cleaning is overdue

inference.explanation: Full recovery every backpulse and a stable weekly average rule out irreversible blocking or overdue cleaning. A breach would raise permeate turbidity, which stays low. Rising feed turbidity fits a reversible cake that backpulse removes.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best confirms reversible cake behaviour?

options.label: Archived cycle TMP traces paired with feed turbidity for the runoff week
Archived CIP chemical log
Archived permeate storage log

nextClue.explanation: Cycle traces against feed solids show the cake forming and clearing pattern.

clueText.nc-a: TMP slope steepens as feed turbidity rises and resets fully after every backpulse.
clueText.nc-b: CIP frequency was unchanged and weekly permeability stayed stable.
clueText.nc-c: Storage levels do not show cycle behaviour.

tasks.prompt: After a module replacement, a train passes its pressure decay test but the overall responsible operator questions whether production can resume.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 3 water treatment plant log. Steady flow unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and maintenance records are available for review.

evidence.label: The replacement module is the same model and rating as the original.
Pressure decay is 4 kPa in 5 minutes, within the 10 kPa limit, on two consecutive tests.
Permeate turbidity is 0.05 NTU and particle counts match intact trains.
Disinfection of the train was completed and documented after the repair.
One required post repair water quality sample result is still pending at the lab.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The train is mechanically intact, but return to service should wait for the pending sample result
The train failed integrity and must stay out of service
Pressure decay results can be ignored if turbidity is low
Pending lab results never affect return to service

inference.explanation: Two passing decay tests plus normal turbidity and particle counts show integrity, so claiming failure contradicts the records. Documented disinfection is complete, but a required sample is still pending, so resuming before it arrives would skip a stated requirement.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best confirms readiness status?

options.label: Archived post repair checklist showing integrity, disinfection, and sample status
Archived train flow totalizer log
Archived feed pump log

nextClue.explanation: The checklist shows which return to service steps are done and which are open.

clueText.nc-a: Checklist shows integrity and disinfection complete with the lab sample still outstanding.
clueText.nc-b: Flow totals do not show sample status.
clueText.nc-c: Pump logs do not confirm water quality clearance.

tasks.prompt: UV reactor validated dose fell below target at the same flow and UVT, and operators suspect the flow meter.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 3 water treatment plant log. Steady flow unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and maintenance records are available for review.

evidence.label: Lamp hour meter reads 10500 hours, past the 9000 hour validated lamp life.
UV intensity sensor reads 62 percent of new lamp output with a clean sleeve.
A reference sensor check agrees with the duty sensor within 3 percent.
Flow verification with a calibrated meter matches the plant meter within 2 percent.
Installing new lamps in a trial restores intensity to 97 percent and validated dose to target.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Lamp aging reduced UV output below the validated dose
The flow meter over reads and dilutes dose
The duty intensity sensor has drifted low
Water UVT fell without being measured

inference.explanation: Hours past lamp life, low output with a clean sleeve, an agreeing reference sensor, a verified flow meter, and recovery with new lamps all fit lamp aging. Sensor drift and flow error are both excluded by direct checks.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best confirms lamp aging?

options.label: Archived lamp hour and intensity trend paired with the lamp change trial result
Archived flow meter purchase record
Archived reactor pressure log

nextClue.explanation: Output against lamp hours plus the change trial is the direct aging test.

clueText.nc-a: Intensity declined steadily with lamp hours and jumped to 97 percent after the lamp change.
clueText.nc-b: Purchase records do not measure output.
clueText.nc-c: Reactor pressure does not set UV dose.
